claims.text: Local chemical disorder in rare-earth-free HEAs induces lattice distortions.
Disorder-induced lattice distortions promote short-range magnetic correlations.
Short-range magnetic correlations enhance magnetic entropy change at low applied fields.
The disorder and associated distortions prevent long-range magnetic ordering and excessive magnetic hysteresis.
Lattice distortions preserve rapid phonon-mediated heat exchange.
Disorder-induced lattice distortions preserve mechanical stability.
An equiatomic 3d-transition-metal HEA can form a highly disordered solid solution with significant local lattice distortions.
HEAs are candidate materials for magnetic-refrigeration applications.
Controlled annealing will reduce local chemical disorder and increase medium-range order.
Annealing can vary chemical order without inducing phase separation or long-range magnetic order.
Nanometer-scale chemically distinct clusters mediate spatially varied exchange interactions.
The as-cast high-entropy state produces spatial variations in magnetic exchange interactions.
Spatially varied exchange interactions foster pronounced short-range spin fluctuations.
Short-range spin fluctuations maximize magnetic entropy change under low applied fields.
A sample with optimized local disorder will have a higher low-field magnetic entropy change than an over-annealed, more ordered sample.
A sample with optimized local disorder will exhibit less magnetic hysteresis than an over-annealed sample.
A sample with optimized local disorder will maintain rapid heat exchange.
A sample with optimized local disorder will retain robust mechanical properties.

The proposed relationship is expected to hold near the magnetic transition and at applied fields below about 1 T, but not necessarily in alloys dominated by long-range magnetic order or different magnetic mechanisms.
Greater chemical ordering should produce lower magnetic entropy change, increased hysteresis, and correlated changes in thermal response.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined ambiguously as either the unannealed, highly disordered state or an excessively annealed, ordered state. The predicted comparison specifically uses the over-annealed state, whereas the falsification rule describes reduced-disorder samples relative to an unspecified baseline; these alternatives can reverse the direction of the disorder contrast.
